prompt.context: Syzygy Supercomputers is a large international fully-integrated computers and communications company with annual revenues of approximately $20 billion U.S. In the past several years, the company has seen a steady decline in profits.
prompt.question: The CEO has asked us to look into this problem. How can Syzygy Supercomputers get back on track?

clarifying_info.q: What additional information is available about Syzygy?
clarifying_info.a: Only the information already provided is available at this time.

clarifying_info.q: What is happening competitively in the market?
clarifying_info.a: There are several players in the market, but everything has remained stable from a competitive standpoint.

clarifying_info.q: How do Syzygy's costs compare to competitors — COGS, SG&A, and other profitability factors?
clarifying_info.a: COGS, SG&A, and other profitability factors are on-par with Syzygy's competitors.

exhibits.title: Syzygy's Historical Costs, Revenues and Profits
exhibits.shows: A chart showing Syzygy's historical revenues, costs, and profits over time
exhibits.data: Multi-year historical financials including revenue (~$20B scale), total costs, and resulting profit trend lines showing declining profitability

exhibits.title: Worldwide Telecom Computing Market (Today)
exhibits.shows: A market share visualization showing Syzygy and its competitors across multiple product categories; rectangles represent market share positions for each player in each category
exhibits.data: Product categories include custom applications, supercomputers, telecom equipment, satellites, and operating software; rectangle heights represent market share levels for Syzygy and competitors

exhibits.title: Syzygy's Absolute vs. Relative Market Share
exhibits.shows: A bubble chart plotting Syzygy's product lines on two axes with bubble size representing Syzygy's total revenues in each category
exhibits.data: X-axis: Absolute Market Share (AMS); Y-axis: Relative Market Share (RMS = Syzygy share / closest competitor share, >1 means Syzygy is market leader); 5 bubbles labeled Product #1 through Product #5

exhibits.title: Companies' R&D vs. Degree of Technical Leadership
exhibits.shows: A scatter plot comparing R&D spending levels to perceived degree of technical leadership for Syzygy and its major competitors, with a normative band indicated
exhibits.data: Syzygy and competitors (including Cray Research and Sonic Wave) plotted; a normative band shows the expected relationship between R&D investment and technical leadership perception

exhibits.title: Syzygy's R&D Expenses and Selling Prices for Supercomputers
exhibits.shows: A chart showing Syzygy's R&D expense breakdown by feature or category alongside corresponding customer selling prices for supercomputers
exhibits.data: R&D expenses in absolute dollar terms by feature type; selling prices or customer willingness-to-pay metrics; highlights gap between R&D spend and revenue-generating features

framework: 1. Examine historical performance: deep-dive declining profits by reviewing revenue and cost trends over time (Exhibit 1)
2. Analyze market dynamics and competitive positioning: assess Syzygy's position across product categories using market share data (Exhibits 2 & 3)
3. Deep-dive profitability drivers: investigate SG&A, COGS, and — critically for a hi-tech company — R&D spending; identify R&D as the key driver (Exhibits 4 & 5)
4. Develop recommendation: address R&D misallocation and evaluate product portfolio rationalization

questions.prompt: Walk through Exhibit 1. What does the historical data tell you about Syzygy's profitability problem?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note the multi-year declining profit trend despite relatively stable or growing revenues (~$20B), implying costs are rising faster than revenues. Should ask to understand which cost lines are growing and request market/competitive context next.

questions.prompt: You now have Exhibits 2 and 3. Which product in Exhibit 3 corresponds to which product category in Exhibit 2?
questions.guidance: Candidate should cross-reference AMS (absolute market share, correlated with height of Syzygy rectangles in Exhibit 2) and RMS (relative market share = Syzygy share / closest competitor share, correlated with ratio of Syzygy rectangle height to competitor rectangle height). Bubble size in Exhibit 3 = Syzygy total revenues in that category. Correct mapping: Product #1 = Custom Applications, Product #2 = Supercomputers, Product #3 = Telecom Equipment, Product #4 = Satellites, Product #5 = Operating Software.

math.setup: RMS = Syzygy market share / market share of closest competitor. RMS > 1 means Syzygy is the market leader.
steps: Identify which Exhibit 2 rectangles show Syzygy as the tallest (market leader) vs. shorter than a competitor
Map each Exhibit 2 product's absolute and relative height ratios to the (AMS, RMS) coordinates in Exhibit 3
Match bubble sizes to Syzygy's revenue contribution per category
math.answer: Product #1 = Custom Applications; Product #2 = Supercomputers; Product #3 = Telecom Equipment; Product #4 = Satellites; Product #5 = Operating Software

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 4, what does it tell you about Syzygy's R&D spending relative to competitors?
questions.guidance: Key insight: Syzygy is the ONLY major competitor whose R&D spending falls below the normative band. Despite spending slightly more than Cray Research and Sonic Wave in absolute terms, Syzygy enjoys LESS perceived technical leadership from customers than those competitors. This is the main anomaly.

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 5, what is the core insight about Syzygy's R&D spending on supercomputers?
questions.guidance: Key insight: Syzygy is spending money in absolute dollar terms to develop features that customers are NOT willing to pay for (i.e., the R&D expense on certain features exceeds any incremental willingness-to-pay). The issue is not the percentage of R&D but the ABSOLUTE allocation — money is going to features with no revenue return.

math.setup: Compare R&D expense per feature to the corresponding incremental selling price / customer willingness-to-pay for that feature
steps: Identify features where R&D expense > incremental customer willingness-to-pay
Quantify the wasted R&D spend on non-revenue-generating features
Note that reallocating or cutting this spend would directly restore profitability
math.answer: Syzygy is spending on features consumers will not pay for; eliminating or redirecting this R&D spend directly improves profitability

brainstorming.prompt: Given the product portfolio analysis (Exhibits 2 & 3), which product lines should Syzygy prioritize and which should it reconsider?

categories.name: Strengthen leadership positions
ideas: Double down on categories where RMS > 1 (Syzygy is market leader) to exploit economies of scale, network effects, and the experience curve
Invest in supercomputers and custom applications where Syzygy has strong relative share

categories.name: Exit weak positions
ideas: Exit Operating Software (Product #5): small and likely shrinking market share will continue to erode due to economies of scale, network economics, and the experience curve all working against a follower
Divesting low-share categories frees capital for R&D reallocation to winning products

categories.name: R&D reallocation
ideas: Cut R&D spending on features that do not generate customer willingness-to-pay
Redirect R&D budget to features customers value and will pay for
Alternatively, maintain total R&D spend but shift composition entirely toward revenue-generating innovation

recommendation: Cut or reallocate R&D spending: eliminate investment in features that customers are not willing to pay for; redirect budget to features with demonstrated willingness-to-pay above the R&D cost

Exit the Operating Software business (Product #5): Syzygy's weak market position means economies of scale, network economics, and the experience curve all work against it — this business will continue to erode
Focus resources on product categories where Syzygy is the market leader to leverage scale and competitive advantages against competitors
risks: Cutting R&D could harm long-term innovation if not carefully targeted — must distinguish value-creating from value-destroying R&D
Exiting Operating Software may have contractual, customer relationship, or bundling implications
Competitors may fill the R&D gap in areas Syzygy de-prioritizes
next_steps: Conduct a feature-by-feature R&D audit to identify and quantify spending on low-willingness-to-pay features
Develop an exit plan for the Operating Software division (divestiture, wind-down, or spin-off)
Assess synergies and cross-selling between remaining product lines to maximize scale benefits in leadership categories
Set R&D spending targets aligned with the normative band in Exhibit 4 and validate with customer research
